title: Repulsion Loss: Detecting Pedestrians in a Crowd
venue: IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition

problem.summary: Intra-class (crowd) occlusion dominates pedestrian detection errors: overlapping pedestrians look alike, so predicted boxes shift onto neighbors, and those shifted boxes are then wrongly merged by NMS or produce high-confidence false positives. Standard box-regression losses only pull a proposal toward its own target and ignore surrounding objects, so nothing penalizes a box that drifts onto a neighbor.
statements: Crowd occlusion significantly increases the difficulty of localizing each individual person in crowd scenes.
Boxes that shift from the target pedestrian onto a neighbor become localization errors and may be suppressed by NMS, turning into missed detections.
Crowd occlusion makes detectors sensitive to the NMS threshold: high thresholds add false positives, low thresholds add missed detections.
Existing regression losses only require the proposal to approach its designated target, without considering surrounding objects.

evidence.quote: Detecting individual pedestrians in a crowd remains a challenging problem since the pedestrians often gather together and occlude each other in real-world scenarios.
The main impact of crowd occlusion is that it significantly increases the difficulty in pedestrian localization.
crowd occlusion makes the detector sensitive to the threshold of NMS
Nevertheless, existing methods only require the proposal to get close to its designated target, without taking the surrounding objects into consideration.

background.summary: Localization is treated as regression over box coordinates: R-CNN used Euclidean distance, Fast R-CNN switched to SmoothL1, RPN regresses anchors twice, DenseBox is anchor-free, and IoU Loss maximizes overlap; on the pedestrian side most work improves filters, features, or NMS, while few prior works study crowd occlusion itself.

evidence.quote: In general, occlusion can be divided into two groups: inter-class occlusion and intra-class occlusion.
In fact, few of previous works focus on studying and overcoming the impact of crowd occlusion.

solution.summary: Repulsion loss augments the usual attraction-to-target term with two repulsion terms: RepGT penalizes overlap (IoG) with the nearest non-target ground-truth pedestrian, and RepBox penalizes IoU between predicted boxes whose designated targets differ, so boxes are pushed away from neighbors and are less likely to be merged by NMS; all three are balanced as L = LAttr + alpha*LRepGT + beta*LRepBox.
solution.approach: Add differentiable penalties that repel each proposal from surrounding non-target ground-truth boxes and from other proposals with different targets, on top of the standard attraction loss.
components: attraction term LAttr using SmoothL1 distance to the designated (max-IoU) target
RepGT Loss penalizing IoG overlap with the most overlapping non-target ground-truth object (Smoothln, sigma)
RepBox Loss penalizing IoU between boxes sampled from different target subsets, reducing NMS sensitivity
smooth parameter sigma controlling sensitivity to outliers; weights alpha and beta balancing terms
baseline detector: Faster R-CNN with ResNet-50 and dilated convolution (1/8-resolution final feature map)
OHEM training with SGD, no multi-scale training/testing for fair comparison

evidence.quote: we propose a novel bounding box regression loss specifically designed for crowd scenes, termed repulsion loss.
This loss is driven by two motivations: the attraction by target, and the repulsion by other surrounding objects.
the bounding box regressor with RepLoss is driven by two motivations: attraction by the target and repulsion by other surrounding objects and proposals.
The RepGT Loss is designed to repel a proposal from its neighboring ground-truth objects which are not its target.
we further propose the RepBox Loss whose objective is to repel each proposal from others with different designated targets.

experiments.summary: A CityPersons baseline analysis (failure-case counts of missed detections and false positives) is followed by ablations of sigma and of alpha/beta, then side-by-side comparisons on CityPersons and the re-annotated Caltech-USA with MR-2, plus a PASCAL VOC 2007 extension measuring mAP overall and on a crowd subset.

benchmarks.split: reasonable, RepLoss (RepGT + RepBox) at x1 scale
test reasonable, IoU=0.5, RepGT+RepBox with CityPersons pretraining
test, crowd subset (intra-class IoU > 0.1), +2.1 over baseline

evidence.quote: The ResNet-based detector achieves 14.6 MR−2 on the validation set, which is sightly better than the reported result (15.4 MR−2 ) in [33].
adding RepGT Loss yields the best performance of 13.7 MR−2 in terms of reasonable evaluation setup.
Combined together, our proposed repulsion loss achieves 13.2 MR−2 , which is an absolute 1.4-point improvement over our baseline.
On a strong reference, RepLoss achieves MR−2 of 5.0 at .5 IoU matching threshold and 26.3 at .75 IoU matching threshold.
when evaluated on the crowd subset (objects have intra-class IoU greater than 0.1), RepLoss outperforms the baseline by 2.1 mAP.

limitations.summary: Gains on PASCAL VOC over the whole dataset are small (crowded subsets carry the improvement), barely-there gains appear on the Bare subset where occlusion is absent, the derivation is restricted to a two-class setting, and the sigma/alpha/beta hyper-parameters are chosen empirically.
items: On PASCAL VOC the gain over the entire dataset is not significant; the +2.1 mAP gain comes only from the crowd subset.
The Bare subset (occlusion <= 10%) shows non-obvious improvement, consistent with the loss targeting occlusion only.
The formulation considers only two-class detection, assuming all ground-truth objects share one category.
Loss balance and smoothing are tuned empirically (alpha = beta = 0.5 best; sigma differs between RepGT and RepBox).

Empirically, α = 0.5 and β = 0.5 yields the best performance.

futureDirections.quote: These results demonstrate that our method is generic and can be extended to general object detection.

equations.name: repulsion loss
equations.expr: L = LAttr + alpha * LRepGT + beta * LRepBox

equations.name: IoG
equations.expr: IoG(B, G) = area(B intersect G) / area(G)

applications.detail: Pedestrian detection is framed as a first step for real-world applications such as video surveillance and autonomous driving, where people gather and occlude each other.
applications.quote: in application scenarios of pedestrian detection, e.g., video surveillance and autonomous driving, pedestrians often gather together and occlude each other.

applications.detail: The loss is shown to transfer beyond pedestrians to PASCAL VOC, with the largest gains on the crowd subset.
applications.quote: Our RepLoss is a generic loss function for object detection in crowd scenes

deploymentClaims: 13.2 MR-2 on CityPersons reasonable (1.4 points better than the 14.6 baseline; 10.9 with larger scale and segmentation).
4.0 MR-2 on re-annotated Caltech-USA test at IoU 0.5, improving the state of the art.
40.8 mAP on the VOC crowd subset (+2.1 over the re-implemented baseline).
Less NMS-threshold sensitivity: a 3.5-point advantage over baseline at NMS threshold 0.35.

evidence.quote: Our detector trained by repulsion loss outperforms the state-ofthe-art methods with a significant improvement in occlusion cases.
Pedestrian detection is the first and an critical step for many real-world applications.
